result:
Solution 1 is correct. Solutions 2 and 3 are not. I could not recall the source paper reliably, so this rests on my own heuristic calculation on the cycle.

On the cycle, a single spike of height x at one vertex spreads like a heat kernel, so its height after time t is about x/√t. It falls below ε only at t ≈ x²/ε². For x of order n or larger, the time is of order n² (up to a logarithm), because of global mixing.

Because ‖f₀‖_p ≤ 1, a spike of size at least x has probability about x^{-p} per vertex. A spike of size x is therefore present somewhere with probability about min(1, n x^{-p}).

The expected time is then roughly the sum over spike sizes x of P(max ≈ x) · x², capped at n²:

- **Typical maximum, x = n^{1/p}.** It occurs with constant probability and costs time n^{2/p}.
- **Rare spike, x ≈ n.** Its probability is about n^{1-p}, and it costs time n². The contribution is n^{3-p}.
- **Intermediate sizes.** For x ≥ n^{1/p}, the contribution is about n x^{2-p}. This increases in x when p < 2, so it peaks at x = n. When p ≥ 2, it is largest at x = n^{1/p}.

Since 3 − p − 2/p = −(p−1)(p−2)/p, we get 3 − p ≥ 2/p for 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, and 2/p is larger for p ≥ 2. So β_p = max(2/p, 3 − p). This matches n² at p = 1 and tends to 0 as p → ∞.

**Solution 1** matches this calculation.

**Solution 2** gives 2/p. It ignores the rare-spike contribution n^{3-p}, which is larger for 1 < p < 2, so it is wrong there.

**Solution 3** gives 2. It assumes bounded ±1 initial data forces n² time, but i.i.d. data with bounded variance averages out on the cycle in polylogarithmic time, so the claimed lower bound is false.

VERDICT 1: ACCEPT
VERDICT 2: REJECT
VERDICT 3: REJECT
